utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be Mr. Peter Bouckaert. It's the Prosecution's understanding that our colleagues from the Defence would like to make some submissions before the start of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Saxon. The submissions will be very brief, Your Honour. This morning we sent the Chamber and the Prosecution a letter which pertains to a number of documents which the Prosecution proposes to use with Mr. Bouckaert. There is a number of documents, I believe about 20 of those, which we intend to object to. They are very similar in nature and purpose to what we say are matters irrelevant to the charges, while otherwise not sufficiently reliable. The submissions of the Defence at this stage are limited to querying the matter with the Chamber as to how the Chamber wishes to deal with these documents, whether the Chamber would wish us to object individually to each document or whether the Chamber would be minded to deal with those perhaps en bloc, which perhaps would be less disruptive of the evidence of Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the en bloc approach sounds more attractive. It puts us simply as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We would be more than happy to do so, Your Honour, having identified the documents which we intend to object to. The only problem we see with that would essentially be for the Prosecution to state the alleged relevance of those documents which we've listed. We hope that we haven't put the Prosecution in a difficult position to do that. We've -- as soon as we received the proofing notes this morning, we sent them the list of the documents which were concerned. I think there are essentially three categories of documents which we object to. They are press articles, a number of press releases, and a number of other documents produced by Human Rights Watch. We have indicated very briefly in our document what the basis for the objection was, either relevance or reliability. Our main concern, Your Honour, is a relatively large number of documents which the Prosecution intends to use with Mr. Bouckaert are not relevant to these proceedings. Our main concern is if this material is permitted to be tendered with this witness, there is a risk that the cross-examination be greatly extended with a view to cross-examining upon those documents should they be found to be relevant, and there's also the risk of additional evidence having to be called by the Defence if the Defence were told that it has to respond in some sense to the evidence which is led through this witness. We don't have a magic formula in terms of practical arrangements for that. It is our belief that indeed it would be easier to deal with them en bloc if Mr. Saxon is reminded to state the relevance of the documents which we listed in our letter this morning. We would be able to respond to each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate that I am told there was a letter received this morning, but something about the letter had the effect that it could not be opened by the Chamber staff; and as a consequence, we have no idea what that letter might contain. We do have, or at least I've just received, the proposed Prosecution list of exhibits, but we do not know which of those are in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I do understand, Your Honour, that there was a problem due to the computer we used the first time to send the letter. Following that, we were contacted by the Chamber and asked to resend the document, which we did resend in a format which we understand was readable in a Word document which should have been provided to the Chamber. I apologise if that has not been the case, but it was done immediately upon being notified. And the document was also sent, I understand, to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it hasn't reached us. So are you able to deal with these matters in the absence of that, perhaps using the Prosecutor's list?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. What I can do, if that's agreeable to the Prosecution, is simply identify for Your Honours the documents which are concerned simply by our letter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to ask for a bit of a break so that we can catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... extra copies here in the courtroom of the memo or letter sent by the Defence this morning, if they could be handed up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you have any copies of your table, this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Additional copies, Your Honour? We have binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is one between three here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we actually have produced a binder for each Judge, and I'm hopeful that we have a binder as well for each Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then, if I could ask you now, Mr. Saxon, whether you feel you would be able to deal with this matter in the way suggested by Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think that I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Splendid. You will excuse us, Mr. Bouckaert, while we go through these technical difficulties. The object will be to make your evidence easier in the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The first document, Your Honour, which is listed in our letter of today is under tab 1 of your binder. That would be Prosecution Rule 65 ter 325, and that's a letter from Human Rights Watch to Mr. Ali Ahmeti, political spokesman for the National Liberation Army. And we indicated in our letter -- the letter is dated the 4th of May of 2001, and we've indicated in our letter that it is the position of the Defence that this letter is, in fact, irrelevant to the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I suggest, Mr. Mettraux, and I'm deliberately going slow for a moment to allow the poor interpreters to catch up, I think as we get excited we speak more quickly and we get ahead of them. It may be able to speed up the process if you were to say, "We object to the relevance of," and then identify the documents you say are irrelevant. We can then hear Mr. Saxon as to the relevance of each of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I shall do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Under tab 1, Rule 65 ter 325 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. If you can, for our purposes, simply say "tab number" would be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perfect. As for relevance, it would be tab 1; tab 2; tab 3 - tab 4 will not be used with this witness, we are being told - tab 7, which also concerns the reliability and related issues; tab 8, which concerns both relevance and reliability; tab 10, which relates to both relevance and reliability; tab 36, which has a more expensive or extensive objection basis; tab 38, several bases of objection again; tab 39, reliability; tab 40, reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As well as relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Tab 40, Your Honour, I believe is limited to reliability. Tab 41, reliability; tab 42, reliability; tab 43, reliability. Tab 44, reliability; tab 45, relevance, reliability, and related issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you believe tab 4 is not going to be pursued?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon gave us this indication shortly before court, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, relevance, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will try to speak slowly for the benefit of the interpreters, Your Honours. Tab 1 is a letter to Mr. Ali Ahmeti, sent by Human Rights Watch in May of 2001. It is relevance -- it is relevant, excuse me, to the existence of an armed conflict in Macedonia during 2001. It is relevant to the notice received by both parties to that conflict as to their obligations under international humanitarian law. And it also explains -- it's also relevant to the rest of this witness's evidence, because it helps to explain and corroborate the work practice of Mr. Bouckaert and the organisation that he represents: Human Rights Watch. Tab 2, Your Honour, which is a very similar letter directed to the then Prime Minister, Ljubce Georgievski, on the Prosecution's submission, has the same relevance; simply a letter sent to the leader of the other party to the conflict in Macedonia during 2001. Tab 3 is a press release entitled "Macedonia Conflict Endangers Civilians," issued on the 7th of May, 2001. And, again, the Prosecution believes it is relevant to the existence of an armed conflict, and there's a note. It's a bit awkward to read; but in the middle of the page, it says: "On Friday, Human Rights Watch sent letters to Macedonian President Boris Trajkovski; Prime Minister Ljubce Georgievski; and the NLA political spokesman, Ali Ahmeti." So, again, this tab 3 is related to tabs 1 and 2; and, again, it provides an indication that at the highest levels of both parties to the conflict in Macedonia, the representatives of those parties were put on notice their obligations under international humanitarian law. Moving on now to tab 7, it is a combination press release and report by Human Rights Watch, issued on the 31st of May, 2001, that talks about violence, if I may say so, systematic violence, perpetrated against ethnic Albanian men by members of the Macedonian police. The Prosecution submits that this document is relevant to the issue of the accused Boskoski's -- to whether the accused Boskoski had known or had reason to know whether his police subordinates had committed crimes in Ljuboten. This document indicates that was information available quite publicly about abuses committed by the Macedonian police well before the events in Ljuboten in 2001; and so in the Prosecution's submission, this document is relevant to the issue of what Mr. Boskoski knew or should have known when there were subsequent published reports about allegations of crimes committed by the Macedonian police in Ljuboten. Tab 8, a Human Rights Watch report and press release entitled "Macedonia, Rioters Burn Albanian Home in Bitula." A subtitle below that: "Police Fail to Stop Violence, Some Actively Participate." In the Prosecution's case, this document is relevant for the same reasons that the document in tab 7 is relevant, and for one additional reason, because it raises the question of the practice of retaliatory attacks on ethnic Albanians after ethnic Macedonian -- after members of the Macedonian security forces suffered losses during the conflict in 2001. And the Prosecution, in its Pre-Trial Brief, refers to the issue of whether the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August were in a way, at least partly, a retaliatory attack. Tab 10 is a press release/report by Human Rights Watch issued on the 25th of June, 2001, entitled "Macedonia, Pamphlet Raises Ethnic Tensions." And the crux of this document is about pamphlets that were found in Skopje in June of 2001 that effectively make a great deal of serious threats against the Siptar population, the derogatory term for ethnic Albanians, and threatening retaliation for any losses suffered by the Macedonian police and/or the Macedonian army. The Prosecution submits, again, that this document is relevant for the same reasons that the documents in tabs 7 and 8 are relevant. Your Honours, tab 36 is a report authored by the witness sitting in front of you, Mr. Bouckaert, detailing the results of his investigation into the events in and around Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001. It is a detailed report based on this witness's interviews with eyewitnesses to the alleged crimes, including with victims of the alleged crimes. And it was also produced via -- the information -- part of the information in this report also comes from a personal visit that this witness made to the village on the 23rd of August, 2001, and where he made observations there. So in the Prosecution's submission, this document is clearly relevant to the issues related to this case. It also addresses the alleged involvement of Macedonian police officers, both reserve and active police officers, in the crimes alleged to have happened in and around Ljuboten. It also makes allegations about the alleged responsibility of the accused Mr. Boskoski and makes strong recommendations to the Macedonian government that a full and transparent investigation into the events in Ljuboten and into the role of the police forces and members of the Ministry of Interior in those events be performed. So in the Prosecution's submission, Your Honour, this particular document, the report in tab 36, is relevant to all counts of the indictment, and it is relevant to the question of whether Mr. Boskoski knew or had reason to know that persons that were subordinate to him in the Ministry of the Interior might have committed crimes on the 12th of August, 2001. If I can turn now to tab 38, this is a press release, Your Honours, distributed by Human Rights Watch on the 5th of September 2001, which I believe was the day when the report authored by this witness was released. And, again, this document is also relevant to the question of notice, whether this accused knew or had reason to know that his subordinates had committed crimes in the village of Ljuboten. And if I may say so, the witness in front of you actually dictated the text of this document as well. There are a number of tabs, really 40 through 44, which are newspaper articles which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean to skip 39?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I did not, Your Honour. I apologise. Thirty-nine through 44 are a -- let me start with 39. Thirty-nine is a report -- a newspaper report published on the 26th of August. It reflects information that this newspaper, "The Sunday Telegraph," had received about the soon-to-be-published Human Rights Watch report about the events in Ljuboten. And it also refers to the fact that on -- this newspaper article, of course, also refers to the alleged role of the accused Mr. Boskoski in the events in and around Ljuboten. The statement of this witness and his testimony will describe the reaction of the accused Boskoski to this newspaper report. So in the Prosecution's submission, this newspaper report is certainly relevant to the issue of the accused's knowledge. And in terms of reliability, it reflects what was subsequently published several days later by Human Rights Watch. And if the Chamber is minded not to accept this document for the reliability of the allegations related to the events in Ljuboten, the Prosecution submits that this newspaper report, as well as the subsequent, I believe, five tabs, 40 through 44, are certainly relevant to the issue of the knowledge of this accused, what notice this accused had about the possibility that his subordinates had committed crimes. If you look at tabs 39 through 44, you will see they all speak to the allegations made by Human Rights Watch in its report, and then 40 through 44 refer to responses by the accused Boskoski. And in the Prosecution's submission, at a minimum, these newspaper reports from many different newspaper media sources, at a minimum, are circumstantial evidence of notice that accused received about allegations of possible crimes committed in village of Ljuboten by members of the Ministry of the Interior. If I can turn now to 45, Your Honours, this newspaper article was published in "The New York Times" ironically on the 12th of August, 2001, and this witness will testify that the information in this article about crimes allegedly committed by members of the NLA against ethnic Macedonian civilians, this information was actually provided by Mr. Bouckaert to the reporter Ian Fisher. Mr. Bouckaert will explain that he was requested by representatives of the Macedonian government at the time to interview victims of the crime that is described in this article; and in the Prosecution's submission, this article then is relevant to the credibility and objectivity of Mr. Bouckaert in the work that he did in Macedonia in 2001. Your Honours, if you have no questions for me, then I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be as brief and concise as my colleague. First, concerning tab number 1, Your Honour, I'll simply point out to you that the document is dated the 4th of May, 2001. That's a time at which Mr. Boskoski was not yet a minister in the government. The same applies to the second letter, the letter to Prime Minister Ljubce Georgievski. So contrary to the submissions of my colleague, this could not possibly be relevant to any issue at any notice. Concerning tab 3, Your Honour, my colleague, Mr. Saxon, has suggested that the matter was relevant to the armed conflict. I do not believe, and it is our submission, that this document, in fact, reflects solely the position of Human Rights Watch, or rather the belief of Human Rights Watch, that there may have been an armed conflict and their understanding that IHL was applicable at the time, but it certainly contains no fact which per se would be relevant to your assessment as to whether that was the case or not. There is furthermore no relevance to the issue of notice, contrary to what the Prosecutor suggested. There is no evidence that Mr. Boskoski, in fact, received that document. Mr. Saxon also has made a comment as to the alleged notice, and you had reason to know this document and others are said to have to this matter. I would say on the line that the charges against Mr. Boskoski are limited to an alleged failure to punish. To that extent, the notice which would be relevant to the charges would be the notice which he received after the commission of any crimes as charged. Mr. Saxon then made a submission in relation to tab number 7, Your Honour. There again, the same submissions by the Defence, the fact that the Prosecution has not established and, as we understand, did not alleged prior to that date that Mr. Boskoski had received that document, and the same submission in relation to the issue of failure to punish. I would also reiterate those submissions in relation to tab 8, adding furthermore that the possibility, which is not established as a fact, that there may have been retaliatory attacks in Bitola, which as far as the document seems to suggest were committed by civilians, would not be relevant to anything that might or might not have happened a few months later in Ljuboten. Tab number 10, Your Honour, the same submission, again, there is no indication that this document was ever received or sent to the Ministry of Interior, and we didn't understand until Mr. Mr. Saxon's submission that this was the case. The same submission again in relation to the issue of notice as concerns an alleged failure to punish. Concerning tab 36, at this stage, I will simply say that this document is indeed a very important document, we understand, for the Prosecution and also for the witness. The same could be said in relation to document 38. What we would propose to do at this stage would be to ask the Trial Chamber to postpone the decision as to the admissibility of this document until after cross-examination so that the reliability of this document, which will be an important issue in cross-examination, could be taken into consideration fully by the Trial Chamber. Concerning tab 38, as I move on, Your Honour, again, the same submission as 37. Concerning the issue of reliability, I would simply point out that the requirements of relevance and reliability are cumulative and that the admission of this document would put the Defence in a position of not being able to test the evidence other than the evidence of Mr. Bouckaert, which could indeed state for himself what he told the journalists, but the Defence would not be able in any way to test the evidence of the journalist or any other information contained in those articles. Your Honour, that would apply equally to the last tab which Mr. Saxon has discussed, tab 45, which is 65 ter Rule 345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you wishing to participate, Mr. Apostolski, in this?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good day. I fully support the presentation of my colleague, Guenal Mettraux, so I have nothing to repeat, and I leave to my colleague Mettraux and Dan Saxon to sort these issues between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon, it is advanced by Mr. Mettraux, among other things, that the only allegation against the accused is of a failure to punish and, therefore, notice should receive a very limited assessment. Do you have anything in response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This morning, I was researching that very issue. The Prosecution submits, Your Honour, that the issue of notice, in a case where the superior or commander is alleged to have failed to punish his subordinates for crimes occurred, the issue of notice does not -- shouldn't exclude events that may have occurred prior to the alleged crimes. In this particular case, the Prosecution submits that the public allegations of abuses committed by members of the Macedonian police during the spring and summer of 2001, prior to the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, would at least provide some indicia to an accused in the position of Mr. Boskoski that when subsequent allegations surface, for example, related to the events in Ljuboten, a person in Mr. Boskoski's position must take those allegations not only seriously but extra seriously, given the widespread reports about similar police practices in the prior months. There is a paragraph, Your Honour, from the Trial Chamber's Judgement in Hadzihasanovic. It is not directly on point on this issue - it is paragraph 166 - and, again, to be fair, it reflects a discussion about allegations of failure to prevent crimes by a commander, not failure to punish. But in the second sentence of paragraph 166, we see this language: "This case also supports the proposition that by failing to punish crimes of which he has knowledge, the superior has reason to know that there is a real and reasonable risk that the unlawful acts will be committed again." Your Honour, in the Prosecution's submission, perhaps at least implicit in that language is the argument that if a civilian leader or a military commander has knowledge of prior crimes, then the superior knew or at least should have known that those crimes might occur again. And if those allegations then -- similar allegations surface again, as they did after the 12th of August in Macedonia, then they would be relevant to the -- to this issue of whether sufficient information was in the mind of the leader or commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Another of the propositions, Mr. Saxon, is that there's nothing to suggest that these documents were ever sent, the documents that are the subject of this submission, were ever sent to the Ministry of the Interior or would have come to the notice of the Minister of that department, and related to that is the fact that there was, for some of the months covered by the newspaper articles, a different minister from the accused Mr. Boskoski. Do you have anything in relation to those matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With respect to the press releases, the Human Rights Watch press releases issued in early May of 2001, before the accused Boskoski became the Minister of the Interior, it is the Prosecution's submission that these -- that the fact that such press releases were sent to the very highest levels of the Macedonian government is at least circumstantial evidence that the Ministers of that government, when they took office, would have received information about these press releases. It is the Prosecution's belief -- it will ask Mr. Bouckaert during his testimony, and it's the Prosecution's belief that Mr. Bouckaert will testify that these press releases and reports were also sent to the office of the Minister of the Interior, but I would have to ask him about each specific report rather than giving you a general offer of proof like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will retire for a short time to consider the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would thank counsel for their succinct and helpful submissions. The general position of the Chamber is that it accepts the submissions of the Prosecution as to relevance, in particular with respect to the three articles published in newspapers in May, the Chamber takes the position that evidence of a general publication which is directed to conduct of a department is information which, on its face, can be expected to be within the knowledge of the Minister of that department and the Minister's immediate successor, that happening very shortly afterwards, and therefore on that basis is able sufficiently to be received at this point, subject of course to whatever evidence comes later which might deal with the issue of the specific knowledge of this Minister. It is also in the Chamber's view, as a matter of fact, that the information published in articles of that nature about the conduct of staff of a ministry is information which ought to put the senior staff and the Minister of that Ministry, and the Minister's successor, on notice of the possibility and prospect of misconduct so that if thereafter, as occurred in August, there are further allegations of misconduct, they may well, as a matter of fact, strengthen the concern that ought properly be expected of the Minister at the time of the subsequent allegations of misconduct. And on that basis, of course, then they have a potential relevance to the knowledge of the Minister in August that is specifically alleged in the indictment. For those reasons, the Chamber would receive the articles as well as the letters that are dealt with, but we would make clear that because they are seen to have both potential relevance and, where that's disputed in respect of Items 7, 8, and 10 in particular, potential reliability sufficient to justify their admission, that is purely for the purposes of the receipt of evidence at this stage. And the Chamber is in no way indicating the view the Chamber will take about these exhibits when it comes to consider the full body of evidence in due course and what is potentially demonstrated sufficiently to justify admission may of course come to be entirely disregarded or treated with very great concern at a later stage, in light of the whole body of evidence. The documents numbered 36 and 38, given the nature of them, in particular document 36, we certainly accept the submission of Mr. Mettraux, that it would be inappropriate to make a judgement as to the admissibility of those two documents at this point, and would therefore take the position that they should be marked for identification and no more until after there has been an opportunity to pursue the issues of reliability in cross-examination. We come, then, to the series of articles at tabs number 39 and following, including document 45, which is, in truth, yet another article. And in the Chamber's view again there is, on the face of it, a relevance to each of these, as they are publications of apparent significance directly concerning the events that are the subject of this indictment, and they're therefore well likely to be of the type to ought to have informed the Minister as to what was being alleged about the conduct of his officers in connection with the events with which we are concerned. The document 45 is also questioned with respect to reliability. We would take the view that it ought to be treated along with the other articles. Essentially, its primary relevance is to the issue of knowledge; and on that basis alone, it is admissible so that we don't need to look further at the reliability of the content, which would of course be informed in due course by the issue of the reliability of document 36. The upshot of that is that leaving aside the document at tab 4, two documents will not be admitted at this stage when tendered but will be marked for identification. They are documents 36 and 38. And the balance will be received, although we once again repeat that that gives no hint as to the view that might eventually be taken of the documents, both as to relevance and reliability, when the whole body of evidence comes to be weighed by the Chamber later in this hearing. Now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, before we begin, I have to remind you and myself that since we both speak the English language, we need to be careful to try to speak a bit slower than normal and to try to pause between my question and your response. That way, we give the interpreters a moment to catch up with us. All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just underline that? We're not merely translating from one language to another. We are, in fact, operating at the moment in five languages, so there are five progressive interpretations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We all understand and we tend to forget. Mr. Mettraux and I were galloping along there at one stage earlier, and the poor interpreters could not keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, do you recall being interviewed by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor during the month of April 2005?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall that your witness statement was finalised and then signed on the 16th of March, 2006?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could ask the usher's assistance, please. We have a copy of the witness's statement, and I'd like to place -- if that could be placed in front of him, please. I need to ask him a couple of questions, and the statement is, I'm told, also available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to paragraph 16 of that statement? It's on the bottom of page 4, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of page 4, we see paragraph 16. It begins with the words: "I issued a press release." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn now, please, to the next page, page 5, because paragraph 16 runs on to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could see the top of page 5. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, the last sentence of that paragraph reads like this: "During the conflict, it became publicly known that the Lions had employment contracts not with the Ministry of Interior but with Mr. Boskoski directly." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there anything in that sentence you wish to correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, there is a typo. It should say "after the conflict." It's referring to the protest of the prior sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, in other words, that sentence, instead of saying "during the conflict" should begin with the phrase "after the conflict"?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. With that correction, does this statement accurately reflect your declaration and what you would say if you were examined orally today?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Witness Peter Bouckaert is a Belgian citizen who has been a senior researcher for the organisation called Human Rights Watch since 1999. Between May and September 2001, Mr. Bouckaert conducted four research missions to monitor and report on the conflict in Macedonia. Mr. Bouckaert's mission to Macedonia, in respect of the events in Ljuboten, took place from approximately 17 to 26 August 2001. Mr. Bouckaert visited Ljuboten on the 23rd of August, 2001. Before and after that visit, he interviewed a number of Ljuboten residents who witnessed the events there on 12th of August, including persons who had been mistreated by members of the Macedonian police. Mr. Bouckaert personally viewed the body of Atulla Qaili which showed signs of severe beating. During his visit to Ljuboten on the 23rd of August, Mr. Bouckaert observed and photographed a number of buildings in Ljuboten that were damaged or destroyed during the attack. During the witness's visit to Ljuboten on 23rd August, 2001, he saw no evidence of the presence of NLA soldiers or defensive positions in the village. During 2001, Mr. Bouckaert documented numerous cases of abuse committed by members of the Macedonian police forces. Mr. Bouckaert also investigated and documented crimes committed by members of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I'd like to ask you some questions about your use of interpreters during the work that you performed in Macedonia in 2001. Did you have a need to employ an interpreter to help you communicate in the Albanian and Macedonian languages at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I don't speak Albanian or Macedonian, so I required an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just briefly, can you describe how you located the interpreter who you eventually hired?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch has been working in Macedonia since the early 1990s; and on my first trip to Macedonia, I went together with our senior researcher for the Southern Balkans at the time, Fred Abrahams, who had an interpreter he had previously worked with. We started working with that interpreter until he had other commitments, and then I found my own interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And the interpreter that you found, did you have to check his English skills?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We interviewed him extensively to test his English skills, as well as his Albanian and Macedonian language skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So this particular person spoke both or, I should say in a triple sense, spoke English, Macedonian, and Albanian?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, he was fluent in all three languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before you hired this person, did you explain the nature of the work that you would be doing?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. He had not previously worked as an interpreter, so we spent a lot of time with him explaining the nature of our work. And it's a standard practice of Human Rights Watch to have this briefing and this kind of mini-training of interpreters. We want to make clear to them, to make them understand, that we're the investigators, they're the interpreters. And especially interpreters who've worked with journalists before, we want to make clear that their job is to translate our questions exactly as they're phrased and to translate the answers of the witness exactly as it was made, without summarising or otherwise interfering in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you insisted on verbatim or word-for-word translation?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, because we're taking statements from these witnesses and we're taking these statements in the voice of the witness, so it's very important that our questions are phrased accurately, but also that the answers are interpreted correctly to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you also explain to a prospective interpreter the principles of Human Rights Watch's work?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Our work covers abuses by all sides, and the interpreter has to be willing to work with different communities. That's often very difficult in the Balkans, and we want to make clear that the people that we work with don't have any political -- strong political views which would make it impossible for them to carry out this work in an unbiased way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if someone -- if a prospective interpreter had indicated to you that they did have strong political views, would that person have been employed by you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The person that you selected to be your interpreter in Macedonia, this person who spoke English, Macedonian, and Albanian, did this person have a university education?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He did a degree in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall the ethnic background of this person?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. He was an ethnic Albanian. The reality in Macedonia is that most Macedonians don't speak Albanian; whereas, most Albanians do speak Macedonian because it's the language often of officialdom, so it was easier to find an ethnic Albanian who had perfect language skills in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall the time period during 2001 when you worked with this interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I started working with him on the first mission that I made to Macedonia, which I believe was in June or late May of 2001. It's in my statement, the exact dates. And I worked with him throughout the conflict. I had a few other interpreters, an ethnic Macedonian and an ethnic Serb, which I used on occasion, but he was my main translator for the duration of my work in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in 2001, did you investigate crimes committed by both sides to the conflict, both parties?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during those investigations of both parties to the conflict, did this ethnic Albanian interpreter assist you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just for the record, are you willing to disclose the names of the interpreters that you used in Macedonia to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It's our policy, as an organisation, not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have a system, Mr. Bouckaert, that you used in 2001 to check the accuracy of the information that you received via your interpreters?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I would take verbatim notes during the interviews in my notebooks; and then after the day's work was finished, I would go through my notes. I would read over the text again with my interpreter to check the accuracy. If I was confused about any particular issue, I would ask him for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if your interpreter couldn't clarify an issue, how would you then clarify the matter?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, one of the nice aspects of working in the Balkans is that everybody has a phone or a cellphone; and during our interviews, we would ask people for their contact information. So if there was anything unclear in the interviews, we would contact the person by phone or some other way and ask for clarification. And some witnesses were re-interviewed to collect additional information or to clarify information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As a matter of practice, Mr. Bouckaert, how many sources would you use for facts that you published in your reports?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It's clear from the footnotes of the report to the reader how many different sources we used. For most of the information, we aim to interview multiple persons and to corroborate the information. That's one of our standard techniques to establish the reliability of information. Our interviews take about one or two hours, and they're very factual. When somebody says, "Fifteen people were killed in my village," we will ask the names and ages of all those 15 people, because it's those kinds of facts which are difficult to manufacture, in case manufactured evidence takes place, and they're easy to check from witness to witness. So times, dates, names, ages, those kind of things is what we focus on in our interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why is it so important to Human Rights Watch, as an institution, that the information that you publish in your reports is accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Because Human Rights Watch is an organisation which is effective because of its reputation internationally. We have access to policy-makers and people who impact on these conflicts because of the reliability of our reporting, and any major error in our reporting, in our research, would have ramifications not only for our work in that specific country but worldwide for our reputation as an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were any of the reports that you wrote about events in Macedonia during 2001 ever challenged due to errors in translation or interpretation?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Not on those bases, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if I can ask Ms. Walpita for an extra copy of the exhibits, which I would like to give to the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, if you could turn to tab 1, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for the record, this is 65 ter number 325. It has ERN N002-5852.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You can see, Mr. Bouckaert, this is a Human Rights Watch press release dated the 4th of May, 2001. It's entitled "Letter to NLA Political Spokesman Ali Ahmeti." Did you have an opportunity to comment on this press release before it was sent?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It precedes my active involvement in the research on the ground, but I did review this letter and make comments on this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were your comments incorporated into the final draft?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the purpose behind Human Rights Watch sending such letters to people like Ali Ahmeti?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, our legal determination was that the conflict in Macedonia had reached a level of an internal armed conflict, so the provisions of the laws of war, particularly Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, apply to this conflict. So we wanted to put all of the parties on notice that they had obligations under international law and also that the Yugoslav Tribunal had jurisdiction over their actions as a deterrent. We wrote this letter as a deterrent and also to put parties on notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This particular document in tab 1 - it's a press release - how would -- would there have been an actual letter sent to Mr. Ahmeti?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. This is the actual letter which was sent to Mr. Ahmeti on May 4th. I believe the press release comes later in tab 3, which was sent two days later. We made public these letters with the press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But you also made public the letter, in a sense, on the Human Rights Watch website?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn to tab 2, Mr. Bouckaert, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 326. It has ERN number N002-5854.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is another letter. It's a letter to the Macedonian Prime Minister, Ljubce Georgievski, same date, May 4th, 2001. Was this letter, Mr. Bouckaert, sent for the same purpose as the previous letter that we saw?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to comment on drafts of this letter before it was finalised?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I commented on the language about the Geneva Conventions. I did not comment on the specific allegations about abuses, which are contained in paragraph 4 of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were your comments incorporated into the final version?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then an identical letter was also sent to the president of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time, it was Boris Trajkovski?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The late president, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The late Boris Trajkovski. If you can turn, Mr. Bouckaert, to what is tab 3 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 327. It has ERN number N002-5856.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a document which I believe you previously referred to as "the press release." It's entitled "Macedonia Conflict Endangers Civilians." It's dated 7th of May, 2001, and there in the middle we see the indication that: "On Friday, Human Rights Watch sent letters to Macedonian President Boris Trajkovski; Prime Minister Ljubce Georgievski; and the NLA political spokesman, Ali Ahmeti, urging that both sides to the conflict respect civilian immunity. Tell us, please, what was the purpose of issuing a press release?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was to let the wider public as well as diplomats and various authorities know that we had sent these letters. It's a very standard practice of Human Rights Watch at the onset of conflict to remind the parties of their obligations. We did similar letters to Israel and Lebanon and Hezbollah last year as well, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned it was to let the wider public as well as diplomats and various authorities know, and I'm just wondering if you can help us, please, with that last phrase: "diplomats and various authorities." Why was it important that diplomats and other authorities know about the letters sent by Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, this press release, which was released together with the letters, made this information, including the language of the letters, available to the press. So we feel that by -- the wider distribution, by making the issue of compliance to international law an issue known to the public, an issue of debate within the country of Macedonia as well as within the International Community, that it would make those issues part of the public agenda, and so exert greater pressure on all parties to the conflict to adhere to their obligations under the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, when you refer to, then, diplomats, for example, these would be diplomats working in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Working in Macedonia, working at the European Union level, at the OSC level, at the UN level, on all of these -- on the issue of Macedonia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We will skip tab 4, and if we could turn to tab 5, please. Tab 5 is from 65 ter number 197. It is a photograph with ERN number N001-4906. Well, that's not the photograph I was hoping to see, but it will have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, do you recognise the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. That was taken by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does it show?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It shows an ethnic Albanian man and bruises from a beating he received at the police station in Kumanovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps if I could ask the Court Officer's assistance, if we could see more of the lower end of the photograph, please. Thank you. Now it's the photograph I was hoping to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you take this photograph as part of your investigations in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why -- and after you took the photograph, did you interview this person about how he received these injuries?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I interviewed him before I took the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did this person tell you who inflicted the injuries upon him?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They were police officers at the Kumanovo police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you began to investigate the events in Ljuboten after the 12th of August, 2001, did information like that given by this victim have an affect or influence in any way your assessment of persons who you interviewed in relation to the incidents in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They helped me assess the credibility of the witnesses that I interviewed from Ljuboten, because their allegations were consistent with many of the cases of police abuse that I had documented in the police stations of Kumanovo, Skopje, and Tetovo, which are the three main police districts in the north of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 6 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert. This is another photograph from 65 ter 197. It has ERN number N001-4908.08.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall where you were when you took it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Kumanovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It's another man who was part of the same large group of people who was beaten at the Kumanovo police station, roughly the same period of time as the previous person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the person whose back is depicted in this photograph, did he describe to you who inflicted his injuries?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We took a long statement from him, and he was also beaten by police officers at the Kumanovo police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P327, Your Honours. Mr. Mettraux, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Simply, if my colleague Mr. Saxon could ask the witness to state the date at which he's taken the picture. The witness has indicated that both pictures were more or less from the same time. We would be assisted if we knew when that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe it would be discussed --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to state the date from memory or would it be helpful for you to turn to the relevant paragraphs of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It was in the last week of May. I would -- it's probably more accurately described in my statement, if I look at my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But it was the last week of May 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is that sufficient for counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters ask once again for the audience and for us, the listeners, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour. Would this be an appropriate time to take the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the first break, and we'll resume at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There needs to be a recording in the transcript of a missed exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph under tab 6 will be received as Exhibit P327, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, I see P326 still on the screen in front of us, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe you're looking at 327.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You are correct, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, could I ask you to pause, because we are getting a language other than English on the English channel. So there may need to be a switching. If you could carry on now, and we'll see whether it comes through correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, we still have in front of you what has been admitted as Exhibit P327. Do you recall the ethnicity of the person whom we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. This person and all of the other people we interviewed were ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if we also refer to the previous photograph, which was given Exhibit number P326, that was also an ethnic Albanian?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, did you decide to write up the results of your investigation into these abuses?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the speed with which this conflict was evolving, we conducted investigations and released our findings soon thereafter, because we wanted to bring these matters to the attention of the Macedonian authorities as well as to the International Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn now, please, to what is tab 7 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 340. It begins with ERN N002-5879.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At the top, we see a title: "Macedonian Police Abuses Documented," and below that: "Ethnic Albanian Man Separated, Tortured at Police Stations." Below that, we see the date "May 31st, 2001." Mr. Bouckaert, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This is the short report that we produced after interviewing and photographing many of the men that we saw in the previous pictures, summarising our findings of what was happening at the Kumanovo and also at the Skopje police stations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I wrote it, together with my co-researcher, senior researcher, Fred Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And subsequently did you or Mr. Abrahams -- after this report was made public, did you or Mr. Abrahams appear in the media or on television in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. This report was covered quite extensively in the local press, both in the Albanian and Macedonian print press, and it also led to an interview of Mr. Abrahams on the ethnic Macedonian A1 television channel, where some of the photographs were shown and Mr. Abrahams was interviewed about the conclusions of our research.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were there other occasions, in the time period after the publication of this report, where you and Mr. Abrahams were persons in Macedonia demonstrated interest in the work you and Mr. Abrahams had done?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. We were approached on at least two separate occasions while we were having dinner in the capital Skopje by ethnic Macedonians who wanted to discuss or dispute our findings following the television interview, so it was quite well known within the Macedonian public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear, you mentioned two separate occasions while you were having dinner in Skopje. Does that indicate you were having dinner in a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. At a public restaurant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this report, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, if you could turn, please, to what is tab 8 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 343. It has -- begins with ERN N002-5888.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a document entitled "Macedonia Rioters Burn Albanian Homes in Bitola. Police Fail to Stop Violence, Some Actively Participate." It has a date 6th of June, 2001. What is this document, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: This document is a summary of our research into an incident in the southern city of Bitola in which the local population or a local mob, which included police officers, rioted following the killings of several ethnic Macedonian policemen near the town of Tetovo just the day prior to this incident, in which eight policemen were killed, including four policemen from the town of Tetovo. And these rioters burned down many ethnic Albanian homes, including the homes of some of the most prominent ethnic Albanians living in Bitola.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn -- can we turn, please, to the second page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It has ERN N002-5889.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see, in the middle of the page, there's a paragraph that begins with: "Human Rights Watch called." Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says this: "Human Rights Watch called on the Macedonian Ministry of the Interior to carry out an immediate investigation into the conduct of the Bitola police during the riots and urge the international community to assist and participate in the investigation." The next paragraph says: "'The conduct of the Bitola police in yesterday's riots is deeply worrying,' said Cartner. 'The Interior Ministry and the international community need to act now to prevent a further deterioration in police discipline.'" Who was this person with the surname Cartner?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That would be Holly Cartner. She was at the time the executive director of the Europe and Central Asia Division which had, as part of its geographic mandate, a Human Rights Watch covering Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That would be myself and Fred Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the intent of the publication of this report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We wanted to get the summary of our detailed investigation, which included a site visit to Bitola and many testimonies that we had taken from ethnic Albanians affected by the violence, out into the public and to try to prevent, as the quote you just read indicates, a further deterioration of the police and discipline and urge the Macedonian authorities to ensure that the police took their duty to protect the ethnic Albanian population serious during such incidents and would not participate actively in acts of violence against the ethnic Albanian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Bouckaert, to which member or members of the Macedonian government at this time, June 2001, this report was sent to?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The sending of reports was done by our New York office, so I was not directly involved in this; but according to my recollection, it was definitely sent to the Ministry of Information in Macedonia, to the UN mission in New York, to the Prime Minister's office, and to the President's office. And I also assume, but I can't confirm, that it was sent directly to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we leave Exhibit 329, was the information in your report -- in this particular report about the events in Bitola also discussed in the Macedonia media?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. It received very prominent coverage in the ethnic Albanian media and more limited coverage in the ethnic Macedonian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to what is tab 9 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 197. It's a photograph bearing ERN N001-4912.19 -- or "-19," I should say. Can you tell us, please, what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. In late June, there was an incident in Skopje where some ethnic Albanian shops had been attacked, and I went to investigate and found this flyer posted on a number of windows in this ethnic Albanian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see a stamp or a symbol on the bottom of it, and can you tell what is depicted in that stamp?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: The stamp has a lion at the center, a sun above it, and the letters in Cyrillic alphabet "MP," which is the initials of what it says on the top also, and "2000" below it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And those words at the top, do you know what it says?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It says: "Macedonian Paramilitary, 2000."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware of the significance of the symbol of the sun and the lion in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, the sun is a very important symbol. It's included on the Macedonian flag, which is a yellow sun on a red background, and the lion was also the name of a paramilitary group in Macedonia which went by the name of "the Lions."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why were you concerned when you saw this particular flyer or pamphlet, if you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, because the flyer made very serious threats against the ethnic Albanian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How would you describe what you observed of the inter-ethnic relations or tensions at that time in the summer of 2001 in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Well, I have worked in conflict zones around the world and also worked in Kosovo prior to working in Macedonia, and the intercommunal relationships between ethnic Macedonians and ethnic Albanians at the time were some of the tensest and the most violent that I had seen up to that point and that I have seen to date. It was an incredibly explosive situation in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall anything in particular that happened the day or the evening when you found this pamphlet?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. On this day, US-led NATO forces evacuated a group of armed NLA members from the town of Aracinovo after a long battle with Macedonian forces which involved helicopters and heavy shelling. On that evening, there was a riot in Skopje which turned very violent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall who or whom participated in that riot that evening?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes. I recall standing in a hotel in downtown Skopje after several journalists had been beaten up by the crowd, international journalists. I believe there was a journalist from CNN who was beaten unconscious. I watched as another journalist from the BBC, who had gone outside the hotel, was running back into the hotel, being kicked by ethnic Macedonians who were chasing him. And at some point a large group of Macedonian police, in uniform, walked in formation down the street, holding a huge Macedonian flag to join the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were these Macedonian police officers, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall what they were armed with?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: They were armed with automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How do you know the uniforms they were wearing were police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Because they were the standard uniforms used by the police. They were green camouflaged uniforms with the badge of the Macedonian police on the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, did these police officers who joined the demonstration do with their automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I was on the phone with the deputy director of the Europe and Central Asia Division as the night fell in Skopje, explaining to her that there was a very explosive situation, that there were rioters in the street, when very heavy gunfire broke out in the area of the hotel. I should explain. The hotel is located just before the largest public space in Skopje, and on the other side of this large public space is the Parliament building. And the firing was taking place in this public space. We were at the hotel, so we couldn't directly see what was happening, if there was an attack on the Parliament or if the gunmen were just firing in the air, but we later found out that they were just firing into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned the deputy director of the Europe and Central Asia Division. Just so the record is clear, that's a division of Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct. And, obviously, because of the situation, I was not staying at this hotel. I wanted to inform them about the security problems that I was facing, the potential security problems, and also update them on the situation in Skopje at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this photograph be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P330, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you turn to what is tab 10 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert, which is 65 ter number 328.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It has ERN number N002-5857.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you decide to do after you found the flyer or the pamphlet that we looked at a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: I had the translation of the flyer available to me at the time. It had already been sent to New York. So I -- we were already in the process of putting out a press statement about the flyer, and we then also included some information about what was happening in Skopje that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, just briefly, how was what we have in front of us -- it's entitled "Macedonia Pamphlet Raises Ethnic tensions." It's dated the 25th of June, and then down below we see: "Macedonia Paramilitary 2000 Order." And the text below that, was that the text of the flyer that we see?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So we see orders to Siptars to leave within three days. For Siptars from Aracinovo, the deadline is 24 hours. After this deadline, all the shops will be burned. If someone tries to protect them, the same will be killed without warning. "We informed Siptars of the Macedonian Republic that for every killed police officer or soldier, 100 Siptars who do not have citizenship or who took citizenship after 1994 will be killed." Do you see what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does this correspond to your memory of what the flyer said?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How was this particular press release or report created? How did your superiors or colleagues at Human Rights Watch then get this information?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: We finalised the text of this press release by me reading it over a cellphone while I was laying on the ground of a hotel room in the dark because of the shooting that was still taking place outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, what was the purpose of issuing this report?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Because if you look at the third paragraph of the press release, it says: "We informed Siptars who do not have citizenship or got it after 1994 to leave Macedonia before June 25th this year at midnight. After this deadline, we will start with the cleansing. The longest night courtesy of Macedonia paramilitary 2000." If you look at the date of the press release, it is dated June 25th, the date referred to in the statement from the paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I thank you for that. I'm not quite sure if you've answered my question. The purpose of issuing this report, as a Human Rights Watch report, was what?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: To bring public attention to the fact that these threats against the ethnic Albanian community had been made by a paramilitary group and also to stress that violence had actually broken out in Skopje on the date stated in this threatening flyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender now the photograph in tab 9 and the report that is at tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will not object, again, to this particular document, but we would be grateful to our colleague, Mr. Saxon, if he could specify the alleged relevance of that document. It was stated earlier, when we discussed the admissibility, a priori, of this document, at this stage what we understand from the evidence, which was clear on that point by the witness, was there were threats made, as he understood, from a paramilitary group. The Defence does not see what the relevance of those threats are to the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Shall I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in the Prosecution's submissions, the state of ethnic tensions between the ethnic Albanian and the ethnic Macedonian communities are certainly relevant to the allegations in the indictment in this case. And we also see, in the first paragraph, the report mentions army and special police forces were seen joining the crowd which took over the Parliament building. Again, we feel that such a public notice is relevant to the information and knowledge that was available to the accused Mr. Boskoski at the time of the events in Ljuboten in August 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, simply a matter of precision English and to the notice which the Prosecution is required to establish. The notice which is relevant to charges such as the charges brought by the Prosecution is that crime - and I'm citing of memory from the Appeals Chamber decision in Krnojelac - that the Prosecution has the burden to establish that the notice given at the time, if established, was that to the effect that a crime similar to those charged in the indictment had or were about to be committed. In this case, there is no suggestion, as I understand, of anyone or any member of the Ministry of the Interior having partaken in any such crime or any indication that would have given any such notice to anyone who would have known about those particular incidents or the claims made by Human Rights Watch in its press release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe we are waiting for a decision from the Chamber as to whether --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document tendered, both of them, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P330 will become Exhibit P330. 65 ter 328 will become Exhibit P331. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you turn, please, to what is tab 11 in your binder --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you turn to what is tab 11 in your binder, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a photograph from 65 ter 197, and it has ERN number N001-4923-05.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Wait one minute. We need to see it to come up on the computer screen. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Bouckaert, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you took it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT
utterances.text: It will be around August 7 or 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The person who we see in this photograph, can you recall his ethnicity?
